templates.pattern: A radioactive source has an initial activity of [A0] Bq and a half life of [THALF] years. Calculate the activity after [N] half lives in Bq.
templates.explanation:
Activity after n half lives:
A = A₀ ÷ 2ⁿ
= [A0] ÷ 2^[N]
= [A0] ÷ [pow(2,N)]
= [RESULT] Bq

This is equivalent to A₀ × (0.5)ⁿ. The half life tells us how long each halving takes but not how many halvings occur.

templates.pattern: A radioactive sample has an initial mass of [M0] g and a half life of [THALF] days. Calculate the mass remaining after [N] half lives in grams.
templates.explanation:
Mass remaining = M₀ ÷ 2ⁿ
= [M0] ÷ 2^[N]
= [M0] ÷ [pow(2,N)]
= [RESULT] g

The mass of the radioactive isotope decreases with each half life. The total mass of all nuclei (parent and daughter) is conserved.

templates.pattern: A radioactive source has a half life of [THALF] years. Calculate the time elapsed after [N] half lives in years.
templates.explanation:
Time elapsed = number of half lives × half life
= [N] × [THALF]
= [RESULT] years

Knowing the half life and the number of half lives that have elapsed tells us exactly how much time has passed. This is used in radioactive dating.

templates.pattern: A radioactive nucleus has [N0] atoms initially. After [N] half lives calculate the number of radioactive nuclei remaining.
templates.explanation:
Number of nuclei remaining = N₀ ÷ 2ⁿ
= [N0] ÷ 2^[N]
= [N0] ÷ [pow(2,N)]
= [RESULT]

The number of radioactive nuclei decreases exponentially. As nuclei decay they produce daughter nuclei of a different element.

templates.pattern: A nucleus has a binding energy of [BE] MeV and a mass number of [A]. Calculate the binding energy per nucleon in MeV.
templates.explanation:
Binding energy per nucleon = total binding energy ÷ mass number
= [BE] ÷ [A]
= [RESULT] MeV

Binding energy per nucleon is a measure of nuclear stability. Iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon at about 8.8 MeV and is therefore the most stable nucleus.

templates.pattern: A nuclear reaction involves a mass difference of [DM] × 10⁻²⁹ kg. Calculate the energy released in joules. (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
templates.explanation:
Energy = mass × c²
= [DM] × 10⁻²⁹ × (3 × 10⁸)²
= [DM] × 10⁻²⁹ × 9 × 10¹⁶
= [RESULT] J

This is Einstein's mass-energy equivalence. Even tiny mass differences release enormous amounts of energy. This is the source of energy in nuclear fission and fusion reactions.

templates.pattern: A patient receives a radiation dose from a source of activity [ACT] Bq for [T] seconds. The dose factor is [F] × 10⁻¹² Sv/Bq·s. Calculate the radiation dose received in microsieverts.
templates.explanation:
Dose = activity × time × dose factor
= [ACT] × [T] × [F] × 10⁻¹²
= [RESULT] μSv

The sievert (Sv) measures the biological effect of radiation. Different types of radiation have different biological effectiveness — this is accounted for by the dose factor.

templates.pattern: A radioactive source has an initial activity of [A0] Bq and after [N] half lives its activity is [A] Bq. The half life is [THALF] years. Calculate the total time elapsed in years.
templates.explanation:
Total time = number of half lives × half life
= [N] × [THALF]
= [RESULT] years

The activity has fallen from [A0] Bq to [A] Bq which represents [N] halvings. Each halving takes [THALF] years.

templates.pattern: A nucleus has a radius of [R] × 10⁻¹⁵ m. The nuclear radius constant R₀ = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Estimate the mass number of the nucleus using R = R₀ × A^(1/3).
templates.explanation:
From R = R₀ × A^(1/3):
A = (R ÷ R₀)³
= ([R] × 10⁻¹⁵ ÷ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵)³
= ([R] ÷ 1.2)³
= [RESULT]

Nuclear radii are of the order of femtometres (fm) where 1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m. This formula shows that all nuclei have approximately the same density.

templates.pattern: A radioactive source has a half life of [THALF] days. Calculate the decay constant of the source in per day.
templates.explanation:
Decay constant λ = 0.693 ÷ T½
= 0.693 ÷ [THALF]
= [RESULT] per day

The decay constant gives the probability of a nucleus decaying per unit time. A larger decay constant means faster decay and therefore a shorter half life.
